opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think politics is the domain where the gap between what we could know and what actually drives decisions is unusually large. In a lot of areas of life, like business or engineering, there are pretty strong feedback loops. If you build a bridge badly, it falls down; if your company makes bad forecasts, it loses money and gets outcompeted. Those pressures push people toward accuracy.

In politics and policy, those feedback loops are much weaker and much more distorted. Voters face the classic rational ignorance problem: any one person's vote is very unlikely to be decisive, so there's little personal payoff to investing in getting the facts right. And there is a real payoff to holding beliefs that signal loyalty to your team. So you get motivated reasoning on a massive scale. People's empirical beliefs about things like the effects of the minimum wage, crime policy, or climate change end up tracking their political identity much more than the evidence.

Politicians and pundits face similar incentives. A commentator who makes confident, tribally satisfying predictions often does better than one who's carefully calibrated, and there's very little systematic tracking of who was right. Philip Tetlock's work showed that many expert political forecasters did barely better than chance, and they weren't held accountable for it.

Now imagine you have AI systems that are demonstrably well calibrated, with a track record you can check across thousands of questions, and that are trained to give honest probability estimates rather than to please a particular audience. That could be a big deal, because the bottleneck in a lot of policy debates isn't values. It's disagreement about factual and causal questions: what will happen if we pass this law, how likely is this conflict to escalate, what are the actual effects of this program? If you could get trusted, neutral answers to those questions, a lot of disagreement would shrink, and the remaining fights would be over genuine value differences, which is a healthier kind of debate.

There's also a scale argument. Government decisions affect enormous amounts of resources and people's lives, and the stakes are getting higher as we move into a period of rapid technological change, including AI itself. Getting things like pandemic preparedness, nuclear risk, or AI governance wrong could be catastrophic. So even modest improvements in the epistemic quality of policymaking could be extremely valuable.

Of course, the hard part is trust and adoption. An AI forecaster is only useful if people across the spectrum believe it isn't biased, so you need transparency, verifiable track records, and ideally multiple independent systems that converge. But if you can establish that, the potential for improvement is larger in politics than almost anywhere else, precisely because the status quo is so far from what good epistemics would deliver.

r001.rationale: It says each voter has little personal payoff for investing in accurate beliefs, describing rational ignorance and weak feedback loops.

r002.rationale: It says people gain from beliefs that signal loyalty to their political team and that empirical beliefs track political identity.

r003.rationale: It describes motivated reasoning and incentives that make political beliefs follow identity rather than evidence, including on factual questions such as policy effects.

r004.rationale: It argues that trusted neutral answers could reduce factual disagreement and that better policymaking could be valuable, but does not clearly claim that providing unbiased estimates throughout the policy process would systematically yield large improvements in policy outcomes.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key thing to notice is that in politics and policy, the quality of decision-making is often not limited by the lack of information in the world. It's limited by the fact that the information isn't credibly shared, and that the people making the decisions, and the people voting on them, have no cheap way to check who's telling the truth. So when a government is debating a tax change, or a pandemic response, or a military intervention, there are experts who have reasonably good forecasts about what will happen. But their forecasts are mixed in with the forecasts of partisans, lobbyists, and people who are just confidently wrong, and the audience can't easily tell them apart. And the incentives for politicians are often to say what plays well rather than what's true, because the voters can't tell the difference, and the consequences only show up years later, when it's hard to attribute them.

Now compare that to a domain like, say, a hedge fund. If you make bad predictions, you lose money fairly quickly, and so there's intense selection pressure for calibration. Politics has almost none of that feedback. Motivated reasoning is cheap, and there's basically no penalty for it. That's exactly the kind of environment where an unbiased, well-calibrated forecaster could have a lot of leverage, if people could trust it.

So imagine you have AI systems that are demonstrably good at forecasting, with a track record you can verify, and that are the same system available to everyone, regardless of which party they belong to. Then when there's a policy debate, each side can ask the same model, "What happens if we do X?" and get the same answer. That changes the dynamics enormously. It becomes much harder for someone to claim that a policy will have great effects when the shared forecaster says it won't. It's similar to how we now treat, say, the CBO scoring a bill, or an independent central bank, but far more general and far more accurate, and potentially applied to every question rather than a narrow set.

And I think the gains from that are extraordinarily large, because the stakes in policy are extraordinarily large. The difference between a well-managed and a badly managed response to a pandemic, or a financial crisis, or an arms race, is measured in trillions of dollars and millions of lives. A lot of those failures come down to decision-makers either not knowing, or being able to pretend not to know, what the likely consequences are. If you can take that excuse away, if the counterfactuals are known and public, then a lot of the worst decisions become politically very costly to make.

The other piece is that this is something where even the actors with power have reason to want it. Governments want to know what's going to happen. Even an authoritarian leader would like accurate forecasts about the economy, or about whether a war will go well. So the demand for this exists, and the main barrier is building systems whose epistemic track record is strong enough and transparent enough that people across the political spectrum can accept them as a common reference point, rather than just another partisan voice. That's hard, but it's the kind of hard that AI is unusually well positioned to solve, because you can test calibration on huge numbers of questions, and the same model can be audited by everyone.

r001.rationale: The response describes weak feedback and cheap motivated reasoning, but does not identify low effort by most political participants as a reason for room to improve.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that political engagement often serves to express social identity.

r003.rationale: It says politicians are incentivized to say what plays well rather than what is true, while voters lack a cheap way to check claims and consequences are hard to attribute. Shared, verifiable forecasts are presented as a way to address this.

r004.rationale: It argues that broadly available, unbiased forecasts and public counterfactuals could make bad policy decisions politically costly and yield extraordinarily large gains given the stakes.

astra-6.text:
Well, politics is an area where people have unusually strong incentives to believe things that aren’t true, or to say things they don’t believe. If you’re evaluating a policy associated with your party, you have some motivation to think it will work. And as an individual voter, you bear almost none of the cost of being wrong about that. Your vote is very unlikely to change the outcome, whereas disagreeing with your friends or political allies can have an immediate social cost.

So there’s potentially a lot of room for improvement from having forecasts that are less sensitive to those pressures. You could ask: If we adopt this policy, what happens to employment? What happens to mortality? What happens to the budget? And you could assess the forecasting system’s track record across many questions, rather than trusting it because its explanations sound congenial to you.

That doesn’t eliminate disagreements about values. People can agree about what a policy will do and still disagree about whether it’s good. But a lot of political argument involves factual claims about consequences, and better forecasts could help narrow those disagreements.

Of course, you don’t get unbiased forecasts just by using AI. The system could be trained to flatter its users or advance a particular agenda. The promising possibility is that you can build systems whose accuracy is demonstrable, and make that expertise available very cheaply. That could give many more people access to a reasonably independent assessment of the claims political actors are making.

r001.rationale: The response discusses weak voter incentives to be right, but does not identify low effort by most political participants as a source of room for improvement.

r002.rationale: It mentions social costs of disagreeing with friends or political allies, but does not say political engagement serves to express social identity.

r003.rationale: It says political incentives can lead people to believe or say things that are untrue, and points to factual policy consequences such as employment, mortality, and budgets.

r004.rationale: The response says better forecasts could narrow disagreements and improve access to assessments, but does not claim that best estimates throughout the policy process would systematically produce large improvements in policy outcomes.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, politics is an area where the incentives to form accurate beliefs are often quite weak. If I’m making an investment or deciding how to run a business, being wrong can be quite costly to me. If I’m a voter, the chance that my individual vote changes the outcome is tiny. So I can get the benefits of believing things that are congenial to my ideology or my social group without bearing much of the cost of those beliefs being mistaken.

And there are similar problems on the supply side. Politicians and media organisations have incentives to tell people things they want to hear, or things that will mobilise them. Those incentives don’t necessarily select for accurate predictions about what policies will actually do.

So if you could provide people with cheap, reasonably reliable forecasts that weren’t systematically favouring one political side, that could be quite valuable. You could ask: what would this policy do to incomes, or housing costs, or the probability of a war? And you could assess the forecaster’s track record across lots of questions, rather than just accepting someone’s claim to expertise.

That wouldn’t resolve disagreements about values, and forecasting the effects of policies has real difficulties — particularly because you don’t get to observe both the world where a policy was adopted and the world where it wasn’t. But a lot of political disagreement involves factual claims about consequences. Improving those beliefs could improve decisions that affect millions of people.

r001.rationale: The response says voters have little incentive to form accurate beliefs, but does not identify low effort by most political participants.

r002.rationale: It says people can benefit from beliefs congenial to their ideology or social group, identifying political belief as a way to express social identity.

r003.rationale: It explains that voter, politician, and media incentives can favor congenial or mobilizing claims over accurate predictions, including factual questions about policy effects.

r004.rationale: The response says unbiased forecasts could be valuable and improve decisions, but does not claim they would systematically produce large policy outcome improvements throughout the policy process.
